steps.prompt: Afraid of the math? Read this first.
steps.sub: Almost all of ML rests on just FOUR ideas — and none of them are scary once you picture them. Vectors, dot products, matrices, gradients. By the end you'll know what each one IS and why it powers everything.

steps.prompt: The four ideas, in plain pictures.
steps.sub: Tap each card. This is the whole toolkit.

cards.b: An ordered list of numbers. It places a 'thing' as a point in space. [height, weight] is a 2-number vector — a dot on a graph.
Multiply matching numbers, add them up. One number that says how ALIGNED two vectors are — the basis of 'similar'.
A grid of numbers — a stack of vectors. It transforms vectors: rotate, stretch, project. A layer of a neural net IS a matrix.
Which way is downhill? It points the direction to nudge the numbers to make the error smaller. The compass of learning.

options.t: An ordered list of numbers that places a thing as a point in space.

steps.why: A vector is just an ordered list — [5.6, 60] could be a person's [height, weight], a single dot on a graph. ML turns EVERYTHING — a word, an image, a user — into a vector, so it can all live in the same space and math can work on it. One number alone is a 'scalar', not a vector.
hints: Is it one number, or a list of them in a fixed order?
Think of a dot on a graph: how many numbers do you need to place it?

steps.prompt: Two arrows point almost the SAME way. What does their dot product look like?

options.t: A big positive number — they're aligned/similar.
Zero — they have nothing to do with each other.
A big negative number — they're opposites.

steps.why: Same direction → big positive dot product → 'very similar'. At right angles → zero → 'unrelated'. Opposite directions → negative → 'opposites'. This one number is how search engines and recommenders decide two things are alike.
hints: Aligned arrows agree. Does 'agree' read as big-positive, zero, or negative?
Right angle = 0, opposite = negative. So same-direction = ?

steps.prompt: Which of the four ideas does each job?
steps.sub: Tap a job, then the idea that does it.

items.t: Turn the word 'king' into a list of 300 numbers
Score how similar two product descriptions are
Transform a whole batch of vectors in one neural-net layer
Tell the model which way to nudge weights to be less wrong
Represent a user as a point so we can find similar users

hints: Representing a thing as a list of numbers = vector. Measuring 'alike' = dot product.
Transforming many vectors at once = matrix. Pointing toward less error = gradient.

steps.prompt: Compute a dot product by hand — slowly.
steps.sub: Two tiny vectors: a = [2, 3], b = [4, 1]. Pick the next move each turn.
steps.goal: Dot product of a = [2, 3] and b = [4, 1].

turns.situation: Step 1: multiply the FIRST numbers of each vector together.
Step 2: now multiply the SECOND numbers together.
Step 3: the dot product is the SUM of those products.

hints: Multiply matching positions, then add all the results.

steps.sub: Tap each card — matrices feel abstract until you see them as machines.

cards.b: Feed a vector in, get a new vector out — rotated, stretched, or squished. A function for vectors.

cards.h: A net layer is a matrix
cards.b: Each neural-net layer multiplies your vector by a matrix of weights. Learning = adjusting those numbers.
Matrix multiply is the same op repeated thousands of times — exactly what a GPU does fast. That's why ML needs GPUs.

steps.prompt: The model is wrong. The gradient tells it…?
steps.sub: Picture standing on a hill in fog.

options.t: Which direction (and how steeply) to change the numbers to reduce the error.
How many layers the network has.

steps.why: A gradient is a compass, not an answer. Standing in fog on an error 'hill', it points which way is downhill (less error) and how steep it is. The model takes a small step that way, again and again. It never hands you the answer — it hands you the DIRECTION.
hints: Downhill in fog: you don't see the bottom, but you know which way slopes down.
It's a direction-to-improve, not the final answer.

statements.t: You need years of advanced calculus before you can understand how ML works.
statements.why: No — the four intuitions here (vector, dot product, matrix, gradient) carry you a very long way. Depth comes later, and optionally.

statements.t: A dot product collapses two vectors into a single number measuring alignment.
statements.why: Exactly — multiply matching numbers, sum them, get one number for how aligned they are.

statements.t: A matrix can transform a vector into a new vector.
statements.why: Right — that's its job: vector in, transformed vector out. A neural-net layer is one such matrix.

statements.t: A gradient hands the model the final correct answer directly.
statements.why: No — it gives the DIRECTION to improve, not the answer. The model steps that way repeatedly to get better.

hints: Two of these overstate what's needed or what a gradient gives you.
Recall: gradient = compass (direction), not the destination (answer).

steps.sub: Not graded. Naming where you'll meet these makes them stick.

Which of the four ideas felt least scary now — and where might you use it?
fields.ph: e.g. dot product, to find similar songs

steps.prompt: Build the toolkit: tap EVERY true statement.
chips: A vector places a thing as a point in space
A gradient points the way to LESS error
You must master calculus before learning ML
steps.why: All four core ideas are true as stated. The last is the myth: the intuitions you just learned take you remarkably far — heavy calculus is optional and comes later.
